vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t1.title: OOP Principles (Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t1.simpleConcept: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a software design approach that models code after real-world things. Instead of writing long lists of instructions, you organize programs into objects that contain data and actions. The 4 pillars make systems modular: Abstraction shows only essential controls (like a steering wheel), Encapsulation locks data inside to prevent tampering (capsule), Inheritance lets child classes reuse parent features (specialization), and Polymorphism allows one command to take many shapes (draw circle vs draw square).
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t1.technicalConcept:
Java is an object-oriented language founded on four core principles:
1. Abstraction: Separating essential interfaces from implementation details using abstract classes and interfaces.
2. Encapsulation: Binding data (fields) and code (methods) together into a single unit (class), while hiding internal state via private access specifiers and exposing controlled public getters/setters.
3. Inheritance: Deriving new classes from existing classes using the 'extends' keyword to achieve code reuse and hierarchical classification.
4. Polymorphism: The capability of an action to behave differently depending on the runtime instance, realized through Compile-time (Method Overloading) and Runtime (Method Overriding & Dynamic Method Dispatch).
keyPoints: Abstraction isolates 'what it does' from 'how it does it' using interfaces & abstract classes.
Encapsulation guarantees data hiding and validation via private variables + public accessors.
Inheritance models IS-A relationships; Java supports single inheritance of classes and multiple inheritance via interfaces.
Polymorphism enables loose coupling and runtime extensibility through Dynamic Method Dispatch.

examModelAnswers.question: Explain the four fundamental principles of Object-Oriented Programming with a suitable Java example.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Abstraction:
• Hiding internal background complexity and presenting only the necessary interface.
• In Java: Achieved using abstract classes (`abstract class`) and interfaces (`interface`).

2. Encapsulation:
• Binding code and data together into a protective capsule.
• Restricts direct access to member variables by marking them `private` and exposing public getters and setters for controlled validation.

3. Inheritance:
• Mechanism where a child class acquires attributes and methods of a parent class using the `extends` keyword.
• Promotes code reusability and forms an IS-A relationship.

4. Polymorphism:
• Greek for 'many forms'. One interface, multiple implementations.
• Compile-time: Method Overloading (same method name, different signatures).
• Runtime: Method Overriding (subclass provides specific implementation of parent method; resolved via Dynamic Method Dispatch).

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t2.title: Lexical Issues (Identifiers, Literals, Comments, Separators, Keywords)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t2.simpleConcept: When Java reads your code, it breaks it into the smallest readable tokens like words, numbers, and punctuation. An identifier is a name you give to a class or variable. Literals are raw fixed values like 42 or 'hello'. Comments explain what the code does and are ignored by the compiler. Separators are punctuation marks like semicolons and braces that give structure, and keywords are Java's reserved vocabulary.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t2.technicalConcept:
Java source programs are tokenized into 5 lexical categories:
1. Identifiers: Sequence of letters, digits, underscores, and dollar signs. Cannot start with a digit, case-sensitive, cannot be a keyword.
2. Literals: Constant values categorized as integer (decimal, hex `0x`, binary `0b`, octal `0`), floating-point (`F`/`D`), character (Unicode `\u`), string, and boolean (`true`/`false`).
3. Comments: Single-line `//`, multi-line `/* */`, and documentation `/** */` for javadoc.
4. Separators: `()`, `{}`, `[]`, `;`, `,`, `.`, and `::` (method reference).
5. Keywords: 50+ reserved words (e.g. `class`, `public`, `static`, `void`, `final`, `abstract`). `const` and `goto` are reserved but not used.
keyPoints: Identifiers: Letters, digits, _, $. Cannot start with a digit; case-sensitive.
Integer literals can be decimal, octal (prefix 0), hex (prefix 0x/0X), or binary (prefix 0b/0B).
Java comments include single-line (//), multi-line (/* */), and documentation (/** */).
Separators give syntactic structure; semicolon (;) terminates statements.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t3.simpleConcept: Java has 8 built-in primitive types for numbers, decimals, characters, and booleans. Widening (small to big) happens automatically. Narrowing (big to small) requires explicit casting `(type)` and can lose data or wrap around.

keyPoints: 8 primitives: byte(1), short(2), int(4), long(8), float(4), double(8), char(2), boolean.
Widening is automatic without data loss.
Narrowing casting truncates fractions and wraps integer overflow.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t4.title: Arrays (Declaration, Creation, Usage)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t4.simpleConcept: An array holds multiple items of the same type in one container on the heap. Index starts at 0. Arrays know their own size via `.length`. Ragged arrays have different column lengths per row.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t4.technicalConcept: Arrays are dynamically allocated heap objects. Declaration `int[] arr;`, allocation `new int[n]`. Runtime index checks prevent buffer overflow, throwing `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. Ragged arrays are arrays of arrays with varying row capacities.
keyPoints: Arrays are heap objects with an immutable `.length` property.
Valid indices: 0 to length - 1.
Ragged arrays allocate different row lengths: `ragged[0] = new int[2]; ragged[1] = new int[4];`.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t5.title: Operators (Arithmetic, Relational, Logical, Assignment, Ternary)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t5.simpleConcept: Operators perform computations. Short-circuit `&&` and `||` stop evaluating as soon as the result is known, avoiding crashes. Ternary `condition ? trueVal : falseVal` is a concise one-line if-else.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t5.technicalConcept: Arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %), Relational (==, !=, <, >), Logical (&&, ||, !), Bitwise (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>, >>>), Assignment (=, +=), and Ternary (?:). Short-circuit evaluation guarantees right-hand operand is not evaluated if left operand determines result.
keyPoints: Short-circuit `&&` stops if left is false; `||` stops if left is true.
Bitwise `>>>` is unsigned right shift, filling with zeros.
Ternary operator is `condition ? expr1 : expr2`.

examModelAnswers.question: Differentiate short-circuit logical operators (&&, ||) and bitwise boolean operators (&, |).

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t6.title: Operator Precedence & Using Parentheses
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t6.simpleConcept: Precedence sets the calculation order (multiplication before addition). Parentheses override default rules and make complex equations easy to read.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m1-t6.technicalConcept: Order: Parentheses -> Postfix -> Unary -> Multiplicative -> Additive -> Shift -> Relational -> Equality -> Bitwise -> Logical -> Ternary -> Assignment. Associativity is left-to-right except assignment and ternary (right-to-left).
keyPoints: Parentheses `()` have highest precedence.
Associativity resolves ties at the same precedence level.
Assignment evaluates right-to-left: `a = b = c = 5`.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m3-t2.title: Stack Operations (Push, Pop, Display Class)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m3-t2.simpleConcept: A stack is a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) data structure like a stack of plates—the last plate placed on top is the first one taken off. This lab program designs an object-oriented Stack class with an array, a capacity limit, and a pointer called `top`. It implements three core operations: `push` (adds item if not full), `pop` (removes top item if not empty), and `display` (shows all items from top to bottom).
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m3-t2.technicalConcept:
VTU Lab Program 2: Stack Class Implementation.
• Principle: Last In First Out (LIFO).
• Member Fields: `int[] arr`, `int top`, `int capacity`.
• Initialization: `top = -1` indicates an empty stack.
• Stack Overflow: Occurs during `push` when `top == capacity - 1`.
• Stack Underflow: Occurs during `pop` when `top == -1`.
• Operations:
  - `push(int x)`: `arr[++top] = x;`
  - `pop()`: `return arr[top--];`
  - `display()`: Iterates from `top` down to 0.
• Menu-Driven Loop: Uses switch-case inside while(true).
keyPoints: Stack follows LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) discipline.
Stack Overflow occurs when pushing into a full stack (top == capacity - 1).
Stack Underflow occurs when popping from an empty stack (top == -1).
Pre-increment `++top` is used on push; post-decrement `top--` on pop.

examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Class Design:
• Encapsulate fields: `private int[] arr; private int top; private int capacity;`
• Constructor initializes `top = -1` and allocates array.

2. Operations:
• `push(item)`: Check `top == capacity - 1` (Overflow). If not, `arr[++top] = item`.
• `pop()`: Check `top == -1` (Underflow). If not, return `arr[top--]`.
• `display()`: Loop from `top` down to 0.

3. Viva Questions:
• Q: What data structure does stack use here? A: Static fixed-size array.
• Q: Why is `top` initialized to -1? A: Because array index 0 is valid; -1 denotes zero elements.

  3. Implementing class uses the `implements` keyword and must declare implemented methods as `public`.
• Class `Rectangle`: Contains `width, height`, calculates area and perimeter, and mutates dimensions via the interface contract.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m3-t7.title: Custom Exception for DivisionByZero (try-catch-throw-finally)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m3-t7.simpleConcept: Java catches errors at runtime using Exceptions. While Java has built-in exceptions like `ArithmeticException`, real-world applications often need custom exceptions. In this lab, we create our own custom exception class called `DivisionByZeroException` extending `Exception`. We write a division method that checks if the denominator is 0, explicitly `throw`s our exception, catches it in a `try-catch` block, and uses `finally` to run cleanup code that always executes.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m3-t7.technicalConcept:
VTU Lab Program 7: Custom Exception & Exception Handling.
• Exception Hierarchy: `Throwable` -> `Exception` (Checked) and `RuntimeException` (Unchecked).
• Custom Checked Exception: `class DivisionByZeroException extends Exception { ... }`.
• Five Keywords in Action:
  1. `try`: Encloses code that may trigger an exception.
  2. `catch`: Handles the specific exception instance.
  3. `throw`: Explicitly triggers an exception: `throw new DivisionByZeroException("...");`.
  4. `throws`: Method signature clause declaring checked exceptions: `double divide(int a, int b) throws DivisionByZeroException`.
  5. `finally`: Block that is GUARANTEED to execute whether an exception occurred, was caught, or was not caught.
keyPoints: Custom checked exceptions extend `java.lang.Exception`.
`throw` triggers an exception; `throws` declares it in the method header.
`finally` block always executes, even if return statements are reached in try/catch.
Provides graceful error recovery without crashing the JVM.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m3-t10.title: Wrapper Objects, Autoboxing and Unboxing
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m3-t10.simpleConcept: Primitives like `int` and `double` are lightweight, but Java's collections (like `ArrayList`) and generic algorithms only work with Objects. Wrapper classes wrap primitives into full objects (like packing an int into an Integer box). Autoboxing is Java's automatic feature that packs a primitive into an object for you, while unboxing automatically unpacks it back to a primitive when you need to do math.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m3-t10.technicalConcept:
VTU Lab Program 10: Wrapper Classes & Autoboxing.
• Wrapper Classes: `Byte`, `Short`, `Integer`, `Long`, `Float`, `Double`, `Character`, `Boolean` in `java.lang`.
• Autoboxing: Automatic conversion by compiler of primitive into corresponding wrapper object:
  `Integer obj = 10;` -> compiled to `Integer.valueOf(10);`.
• Unboxing: Automatic conversion of wrapper object back into primitive:
  `int x = obj;` -> compiled to `obj.intValue();`.
• Utility Methods: `Integer.parseInt("123")`, `Integer.toBinaryString(42)`, `Integer.MAX_VALUE`.
• Null Safety: Unboxing a `null` reference throws `NullPointerException` at runtime.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t1.title: Class Fundamentals, Declaring Objects & Assigning References
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t1.simpleConcept: A class is like an architectural blueprint for a house, and an object is the actual house built from that blueprint. In Java, when you declare an object variable, you only create a pointer (reference) on the stack. The actual object data is created in the heap when you use the `new` keyword. If you assign one object variable to another (`b2 = b1`), both variables point to the same house—changing one changes both!
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t1.technicalConcept:
A class is a user-defined composite data type that defines instance variables (state) and methods (behavior).
• Instantiation: `ClassName obj = new ClassName();`
  1. `ClassName obj;` declares a reference variable on the thread stack (initialized to null).
  2. `new` allocates dynamic heap memory for object's instance fields.
  3. `ClassName()` executes constructor to initialize state.
• Reference Assignment: `obj2 = obj1;` does NOT copy the object! It copies the memory address/reference. Both references now point to the exact same heap instance (aliasing).
keyPoints: A class is a template; an object is an instantiated physical entity.
Object variables store reference addresses, not the object's memory contents.
Reference assignment (`b2 = b1`) causes both references to point to the same heap instance.
Memory on heap is reclaimed automatically by Garbage Collector when references reach zero.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t2.title: Introducing Methods & Constructors
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t2.simpleConcept: Methods are actions that an object can perform. They take inputs (parameters), do computations, and return a result. A constructor is a special method called automatically when an object is born with `new`. Its name must match the class name exactly, and it has no return type. Constructors initialize an object's starting values so it never begins life with corrupted or missing data.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t2.technicalConcept:
Methods define behavioral capabilities of classes:
• Method Signature: `returnType methodName(parameterList) { ... }`
• Return type can be any primitive, object reference, or `void`.

Constructors:
• Special initialization routine invoked automatically during `new` instantiation.
• Rules:
  1. Must have the EXACT same name as the enclosing class.
  2. Does NOT have any return type (not even `void`).
  3. If no constructor is written, Java provides a default no-argument constructor initializing fields to defaults (0, null, false).
  4. Once any parameterized constructor is defined, Java suppresses the default constructor.
keyPoints: Constructor name must match class name exactly.
Constructors have NO return type, not even void.
Compiler supplies a default no-arg constructor ONLY if no explicit constructor is defined.
Constructor overloading allows objects to be initialized in multiple ways.

1. Definition of Constructor:
• A special member method automatically invoked when an instance of a class is created using the `new` keyword.
• Primary purpose: Initialize instance variables to valid initial states.

2. Key Characteristics:
• Must have the same name as the class.
• Has no return type (specifying a return type turns it into a normal method!).
• Automatically invoked at instantiation time.
• Cannot be `abstract`, `static`, or `final`.

3. Constructor Overloading:
• Having multiple constructors in the same class with different parameter lists (different number, types, or order of parameters).
• Enables callers to initialize objects in multiple ways (e.g. default dimensions vs custom dimensions).
examModelAnswers.markingTip: Point out that if you put `void Box()` it becomes a standard method, NOT a constructor.

1BCS302_M2_T2.title: Introducing Methods & Constructors
1BCS302_M2_T2.simpleConcept: Methods are actions that an object can perform. They take inputs (parameters), do computations, and return a result. A constructor is a special method called automatically when an object is born with `new`. Its name must match the class name exactly, and it has no return type. Constructors initialize an object's starting values so it never begins life with corrupted or missing data.
1BCS302_M2_T2.technicalConcept:
Methods define behavioral capabilities of classes:
• Method Signature: `returnType methodName(parameterList) { ... }`
• Return type can be any primitive, object reference, or `void`.

Constructors:
• Special initialization routine invoked automatically during `new` instantiation.
• Rules:
  1. Must have the EXACT same name as the enclosing class.
  2. Does NOT have any return type (not even `void`).
  3. If no constructor is written, Java provides a default no-argument constructor initializing fields to defaults (0, null, false).
  4. Once any parameterized constructor is defined, Java suppresses the default constructor.
keyPoints: Constructor name must match class name exactly.
Constructors have NO return type, not even void.
Compiler supplies a default no-arg constructor ONLY if no explicit constructor is defined.
Constructor overloading allows objects to be initialized in multiple ways.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t3.title: The 'this' Keyword & Garbage Collection
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t3.simpleConcept: The `this` keyword refers to the current object executing a method or constructor. It resolves conflicts when parameter names match instance variables (`this.width = width`). `this(...)` calls another constructor in the same class (first line only). Garbage Collection is Java's automatic cleaner that frees memory when objects have zero references.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t3.technicalConcept: `this` is an implicit reference to the calling instance. Resolves parameter shadowing and enables constructor chaining. Garbage Collection runs as a daemon thread in the JVM, identifying unreachable heap objects using mark-and-sweep. `System.gc()` requests GC execution non-deterministically.
keyPoints: `this.field` resolves parameter shadowing.
`this(...)` constructor chaining MUST be the first statement.
Garbage Collection reclaims unreachable heap objects automatically.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t5.title: Argument Passing (Call by Value) & Returning Objects
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t5.simpleConcept: Java is ALWAYS Pass-by-Value! For primitives, Java passes a copy of the number. For objects, Java passes a copy of the reference address. Mutating an object's fields affects the caller's object, but reassigning the reference variable itself never changes the caller's reference.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t5.technicalConcept: Java is exclusively Call-by-Value. Primitives pass a copy of the primitive data. Objects pass a copy of the reference pointer by value. Methods can also construct and return objects to callers.
keyPoints: Java is 100% Pass-by-Value.
Primitives are completely protected from external modification.
Object fields can be modified via reference copy, but reassigning the pointer stays local.
Methods can return new object instances to callers.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t6.title: Recursion in Java
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t6.simpleConcept: Recursion is when a method calls itself to solve smaller pieces of a problem. Every recursive method must have a base case to stop, and a recursive step. Without a base case, it overflows memory with StackOverflowError.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t6.technicalConcept: Method calling itself. Requires base condition and recursive step. Each call pushes a stack frame onto the Call Stack. Missing or unreachable base condition exhausts stack memory, throwing `StackOverflowError`.
keyPoints: Requires a base case to terminate.
Each call adds a frame to the Call Stack.
Infinite recursion causes `StackOverflowError`.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t7.title: Access Control (public, private, protected) & static keyword
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t7.simpleConcept: `private` keeps data inside the class, default shares within the package, `protected` opens to subclasses, and `public` opens to everyone. `static` members belong to the class itself—shared by all objects, and static methods can run without creating any object.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs302-2025-m2-t7.technicalConcept: Access levels: private (class), default (package), protected (package + subclasses in other packages), public (world). `static` variables have single memory in Metaspace shared across instances. Static methods cannot access instance variables or use `this`/`super`.
keyPoints: Access: private < default < protected < public.
static variables are shared across all instances.
static methods cannot access non-static fields or use `this`.
